stem: A newborn girl is hypotonic with upslanting palpebral fissures and a single palmar crease. Echocardiography shows a defect in the lower atrial septum, at the level of the atrioventricular valves.
oneliner: Newborn F + hypotonia + upslanting palpebral fissures + single palmar crease + lower atrial septal defect at AV valve level → ?
ask: Which chromosomal abnormality is most likely?

whyNot.B: Gives **conotruncal** defects (truncus arteriosus, tetralogy); this defect is in the **atrial septum at the AV valves**
whyNot.C: Turner syndrome gives **coarctation or a bicuspid aortic valve**, not a defect at the AV valve level with upslanting fissures
whyNot.D: Williams syndrome gives **supravalvular aortic stenosis**; the defect here is in the atrial septum
whyNot.E: Trisomy 18 gives a **VSD** with clenched fists and **hypertonia**; this baby is **hypotonic** with upslanting fissures

why: A defect at the **AV valve level** is an **endocardial cushion defect** (ostium primum ASD or AV septal defect), and **hypotonia with upslanting fissures and a single palmar crease** marks **Down syndrome**. Ostium secundum, not primum, is the commonest ASD overall.

idea.rule: Endocardial cushion defects travel with trisomy 21.
also: Complete AV septal defect with a common AV valve is the classic Down syndrome heart lesion
Ostium primum ASD often comes with a cleft anterior mitral leaflet
About 40-50% of babies with Down syndrome have a heart defect

stem: A 17-year-old boy faints during a basketball game. Echocardiography shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy. His father had the same echo finding and died suddenly at age 35, and his paternal aunt is also affected.
oneliner: 17M + exertional syncope + asymmetric septal hypertrophy + affected father (sudden death at 35) + affected paternal aunt → which inheritance?
ask: Which inheritance pattern is most likely?

whyNot.B: Usually affects siblings of **unaffected carrier parents**; here a **parent and an aunt** are affected in successive generations
whyNot.C: Spares **male-to-male** transmission; the father is affected
whyNot.D: Passes only through the **mother**; the affected line is paternal
whyNot.E: Multifactorial traits rarely give **affected members in every generation** like this father, aunt and son

answer: Autosomal dominant (sarcomere gene, e.g. beta-myosin heavy chain)
why: Familial HCM is **autosomal dominant** from **sarcomere gene** mutations such as **beta-myosin heavy chain**. An affected **father to son** with an affected aunt gives a **vertical pedigree with male-to-male transmission**; each child of an affected parent has a **50%** risk.

idea.rule: Vertical transmission with male-to-male spread means autosomal dominant.
also: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (endoglin, ALK1) is autosomal dominant
Familial hypercholesterolemia (LDL receptor) is autosomal dominant
Male-to-male transmission excludes X-linked and mitochondrial inheritance

stem: A 2-year-old boy has an isolated ventricular septal defect with no other anomalies. His parents are healthy, both have normal echocardiograms, and they ask the chance that a future child will have a heart defect.
oneliner: 2M + isolated VSD, no syndrome + healthy parents with normal echo → recurrence risk in next child?
ask: What is the approximate recurrence risk?

whyNot.A: Not zero: first-degree relatives have a **higher risk** than the general population
whyNot.C: The figure for an **autosomal recessive** disorder, which an isolated defect does not follow
whyNot.D: The figure for an **autosomal dominant** trait with an affected parent; both parents are healthy
whyNot.E: Would need a **fully penetrant** cause shared by every child; this defect is **isolated** and the parents are normal

why: An **isolated** congenital heart defect is **multifactorial**, from several genes plus environment. Recurrence in a sibling is only about **3%**, far from **Mendelian** risks of 25% or 50%.

idea.rule: Isolated congenital heart defect = multifactorial = low single-digit recurrence.
also: Cleft lip and palate are multifactorial
Recurrence risk for a multifactorial trait rises with more affected relatives

stem: A 45-year-old man has had lifelong nosebleeds and has telangiectasias on his lips and tongue. He now has exertional dyspnea with pulmonary arteriovenous shunting on imaging, and his mother had the same nosebleeds.
oneliner: 45M + lifelong nosebleeds + lip telangiectasias + exertional dyspnea + pulmonary AV shunt + affected mother → which gene?
ask: Which gene is most likely mutated?

whyNot.A: FBN1 defects cause Marfan syndrome with aortic root disease, not **lifelong nosebleeds with mucosal telangiectasias**
whyNot.B: COL3A1 defects cause vascular Ehlers-Danlos with arterial rupture, not **telangiectasias on the lips and tongue**
whyNot.C: NF1 causes cafe-au-lait spots and neurofibromas, not **pulmonary arteriovenous shunting**
whyNot.E: VHL causes hemangioblastomas and renal cell carcinoma, not **recurrent epistaxis with telangiectasias**

answer: Endoglin (ENG), a TGF-beta signaling gene (ALK1 also causes HHT)
why: **Recurrent epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias** and **pulmonary arteriovenous shunts** with an affected parent make **hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia**. It is **autosomal dominant**, from **endoglin** or **ALK1** mutations in TGF-beta signaling.

idea.rule: HHT = autosomal dominant TGF-beta pathway gene (endoglin, ALK1).
also: SMAD4 mutation causes HHT with juvenile polyposis
BMPR2, another TGF-beta family receptor, causes heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension

stem: In a muscle physiology experiment, a protein is isolated from the lumen of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. It binds about 50 Ca2+ ions per molecule and is anchored near the ryanodine receptor.
oneliner: Experiment: sarcoplasmic reticulum luminal protein + binds ~50 Ca2+ + anchored near ryanodine receptor → which protein?

whyNot.B: A **cytoplasmic** calcium sensor that activates kinases, not a luminal store
whyNot.C: Binds calcium on the **thin filament** to trigger contraction, in the cytoplasm
whyNot.D: A **pump in the SR membrane** that moves Ca2+ into the lumen; it is not a luminal buffer binding 50 ions
whyNot.E: A **regulator of SERCA** in the membrane; it does not bind Ca2+ in the lumen

answer: Calsequestrin (a calcium buffer in the SR lumen)
why: **Calsequestrin** sits **inside the SR lumen near the ryanodine receptor** and binds large amounts of **stored Ca2+**, buffering it for release. The other options work in the **cytoplasm or membrane**.

idea.rule: Calsequestrin stores calcium in the SR; SERCA pumps it in; the ryanodine receptor lets it out.
also: Calmodulin binds calcium in smooth muscle to activate myosin light chain kinase
Troponin C triggers contraction in striated muscle
